scenario_reference.text: When operations are submitted to the system at runtime, all of them are processed at the fastest possible speed.

analysis_records.environment: Runtime; sequential event processing on a single processor with input via CLI (AE-6, AE-7); no load level is stated in RS-2
analysis_records.stimulus: Operations submitted to the system for processing
architectural_decisions: All operations enter one Event Queue (architecture_limits.event_queues = 1) and are dispatched FIFO (AP-1, AE-10, BD-11).
One Event Manager (architecture_limits.event_managers = 1) dispatches every event directly to application handlers (AP-2, AE-3, AE-10).
Event handling is spread over a base Handler extended by standard and application-specific handlers (AP-3, AE-5).
Events are processed sequentially on a single processor (AP-6, inferred from AE-7, which the input itself calls 'implied').
analysis_records.reasoning: The input states the performance proxy is the number of components involved in a transaction (AE-8) and that transaction speed is 'Slow due to high number of components involved' (AE-9); this is an observed statement of the problem, not a measurement. No numeric arrival rate, service time or component count is given, so no latency or throughput arithmetic is possible (G-2-2). Structurally (inferred): with one queue, one manager and sequential processing (AP-1, AP-2, AP-6), the time an event spends in the system is its own processing time plus the processing times of every event ahead of it in the FIFO queue; throughput is bounded by a single Event Manager serving one event at a time. No prioritization, parallel dispatch or second queue/manager is described, so a slow handler delays every later event. Whether this meets 'fastest possible speed' cannot be judged because that phrase has no measurable target (G-2-2, G-4-4). The link between the number of components per transaction and the handler decomposition (AP-3) is an inference: the components that make the framework extensible are the ones a transaction passes through.

risks.description: Transactions pass through a high number of framework components, and the input itself states that transaction speed is slow for this reason.
risks.rationale: evaluation_inputs.quantitative_model_parameters.transaction_speed states 'Qualitative (Slow due to high number of components involved)' and performance_proxy names the number of components involved in a transaction as the performance driver; RS-2 asks for the fastest possible speed.

risks.description: The single Event Queue and single Event Manager with sequential FIFO processing serialize all operations, so one long-running handler delays every event queued behind it (head-of-line blocking) and no prioritization or parallel dispatch is available.
risks.rationale: AE-10 fixes 1 Event Manager and 1 Event Queue; BD-11 requires FIFO dispatch; AP-6 (inferred from AE-7) makes processing sequential. Under these decisions an event's waiting time is the sum of the service times of the events ahead of it. Depends on the inferred approach AP-6 (see G-4-5).

sensitivity_points.parameter: Number of components involved in a transaction (cited as the performance proxy, AE-8; qualitatively 'Slow', AE-9; no numeric value given)
Number of Event Managers and Event Queues (cited: 1 each, AE-10) serving all events

tradeoff_points.parameter: Number of components a transaction passes through (base Handler, standard and application-specific handlers, Event Manager, Event Queue); inferred: the decomposition that lets behaviour be varied and extended by handlers is what lengthens each transaction (AE-8, AE-9, AP-3)
Single Event Manager and single Event Queue (cited: 1 each, AE-10); inferred: one ordering and dispatch point gives uniform behaviour but serializes all work and has no redundancy

scenario_reference.text: When a failure occurs while the system is running, the system recovers immediately.

analysis_records.environment: Runtime; no operating condition is stated in RS-3
analysis_records.stimulus: A failure occurs (failure type not stated in RS-3)
architectural_decisions: Exactly one Event Queue and one Event Manager exist (AE-10, AP-1, AP-2); no redundant instance, restart or checkpoint mechanism is described (G-3-7).
The Event Manager calls application handlers directly (AE-3, AP-2), and application logic is embedded in framework components (AE-1, BD-13, AP-4).
Processing is sequential on one processor (AP-6, inferred from AE-7).
analysis_records.reasoning: RS-3 requires immediate recovery after a failure, which makes some detection and recovery mechanism necessary. The inputs describe none (G-3-7), and AE-10 fixes a single Event Queue and a single Event Manager, so (inferred) a failure of either component stops all event processing, with no stated component that would restart it or take over. Whether events in the queue survive such a failure is unknown because persistence is not described (G-3-9). Because the Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers (AE-3) and application logic is embedded within framework components (AE-1, BD-13), no fault-isolation boundary between application handler code and the framework is described; inferred: a fault raised in an application-specific handler reaches the Event Manager directly and, in a sequential single-processor model (AP-6), halts the only processing path. Whether 'immediate' recovery is achieved cannot be judged because no recovery time or target state is given (G-2-3, G-4-4).

risks.description: The single Event Manager and single Event Queue (AE-10) have no stated redundancy, restart or recovery mechanism, so a failure of either stops all event processing, contrary to the immediate recovery RS-3 requires.
risks.rationale: RS-3 makes a recovery mechanism necessary; AE-10 limits the architecture to one manager and one queue and no input or AE item describes recovery (G-3-7). Survival of queued events is unknown (G-3-9, G-4-12).

risks.description: No fault-isolation boundary is described between application-specific handlers and the Event Manager: the manager calls handlers directly (AE-3) and application logic is embedded in framework components (AE-1, BD-13), so a fault in application handler code can propagate into the framework and stop event processing.
risks.rationale: Direct manager-to-handler interaction plus the stated high framework-application interdependence leaves no described point where a handler failure is contained; under sequential processing (AP-6, inferred) the failed path is the only path.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Number of Event Managers and Event Queues (cited: 1 each, AE-10); a single instance is a single point of failure for all event processing
Fault-isolation boundary between application-specific handlers and the Event Manager (direct interaction, AE-3; application logic embedded in framework components, AE-1)

scenario_reference.text: When a user makes an error in using the system, such as giving invalid input via the CLI, the system handles the error.

analysis_records.environment: Runtime; the user interacts via CLI (AE-6); no further condition is stated in RS-4
analysis_records.stimulus: A user makes an error in using the system (e.g. invalid input, per evaluator_inquiry_questions[2])
architectural_decisions: User input arrives through the CLI and the system idles until input is received (AP-7, AE-6, BD-5, BD-12).
Input becomes events placed on the single Event Queue and dispatched by the Event Manager to handlers (AP-1, AP-2, AE-3, AE-4).
Handlers specialize a base Handler (AP-3, AE-5); no handler or component for input validation or error reporting is named.
analysis_records.reasoning: RS-4 requires that user errors such as invalid CLI input be handled, which makes an input-validation and error-handling decision necessary. The inputs describe the path CLI (AE-6) -> Event Queue (AE-4) -> Event Manager (AE-3) -> handler (AE-5) but name no validation step, error handler or error-reporting path on it (G-3-7). Inferred: unless each handler validates its own input, invalid input can be enqueued and dispatched with no defined rejection or report behaviour, and where validation happens (before enqueueing or inside every handler) determines whether the response is uniform. It is possible that validation exists inside handlers in the undisclosed class diagrams (G-1-3, G-3-10); the risk is recorded because the scenario needs the mechanism and none is stated. Whether the handling is adequate cannot be judged because 'handled' is not defined (G-2-4, G-4-4).

risks.description: No input-validation or error-handling decision is stated on the CLI-to-Event Queue-to-handler path, so invalid user input may be enqueued and dispatched to a handler with no defined rejection or reporting behaviour.
risks.rationale: RS-4 makes invalid-input handling necessary; AE-6, AE-4, AE-3 and AE-5 describe the input path but no AE item or approach describes validation or error handling (G-3-7).

sensitivity_points.parameter: Location of invalid-input validation on the path CLI (AE-6) -> Event Queue (AE-4) -> Event Manager (AE-3) -> handler (AE-5): before enqueueing or inside each handler (not stated)

scenario_reference.text: When new demands on system functionality arise during development or maintenance, the system accommodates them.

analysis_records.environment: Development/maintenance time (inferred from the change-oriented wording); no condition is stated in RS-5
architectural_decisions: New application behaviour is added as application-specific handlers extending the base Handler (AP-3, AE-5).
The Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers (AP-2, AE-3); the binding of handlers to events is not described (G-3-6).
Application logic is embedded within framework components and is highly inter-dependent with the framework (AP-4, AE-1, BD-13).
analysis_records.reasoning: Two decisions pull in opposite directions. The handler hierarchy (AE-5) gives a defined extension point: inferred, new functionality that takes the form of handling a new or existing event can be added as a new application-specific handler subtype without changing the Event Queue. How much of the Event Manager must change depends on how handlers are bound to events, which is not described (G-3-6): with a registration or lookup mechanism the manager is untouched; with hard-coded dispatch it must be edited for each new handler. Against this, the input states that application logic is embedded within framework components and that application and framework are highly inter-dependent (AE-1, BD-13); inferred, functional demands that change that embedded logic, or that do not fit a handler subtype, require editing framework components. The event-driven style reading of AP-9 that would localize changes to handlers is itself inferred (G-3-4). The size of change that is acceptable is not stated (G-2-5, G-4-4).

risks.description: Because application logic is embedded within framework components (BD-13) and application and framework are highly inter-dependent (AE-1), new functional demands that touch that embedded logic require changes inside framework components rather than only new handlers.
risks.rationale: The input states the embedding and inter-dependence directly; that this widens the scope of functional change is reasoned from it. No rationale for the embedding is given (G-3-5).

non_risks.description: Functionality that can be expressed as handling an event can be added as a new application-specific handler extending the base Handler, without changing the Event Queue.
non_risks.rationale: AE-5 states that the base Handler is extended by application-specific handlers, which is a defined extension point. Whether the Event Manager also needs changes depends on the undisclosed handler binding mechanism (G-3-6, G-4-7).

sensitivity_points.parameter: Handler-to-event binding mechanism of the Event Manager (static dispatch, registration or lookup table; not described, G-3-6)
Extent to which application logic is embedded within framework components (AE-1, BD-13)

scenario_reference.text: When a future architecture or project is built, major parts of the framework can be reused in it.

analysis_records.environment: Development of a future architecture (inferred from RS-6 and evaluator_inquiry_questions[0]); no further condition is stated
analysis_records.stimulus: A future architecture or project needs framework capabilities
architectural_decisions: The framework parts are the Event Queue, the Event Manager, the base Handler and standard handlers (AE-3, AE-4, AE-5).
Application logic is embedded within those framework components (AP-4, AE-1, BD-13).
analysis_records.reasoning: The candidates for reuse are the framework's Event Queue, Event Manager, base Handler and standard handlers (AE-3, AE-4, AE-5). The input states that application logic is embedded within framework components and that application and framework are highly inter-dependent (AE-1, BD-13). Inferred: components that contain one application's logic cannot be reused in a different architecture as they are; the application-specific parts must first be separated out or removed. The base Handler abstraction is the part least likely to carry application logic, but the inputs do not say which components hold the embedded logic, so no non-risk is recorded. Which parts are 'major' and what counts as reuse are not stated (G-2-6, G-4-4).

risks.description: Application logic embedded within framework components (BD-13, AE-1) ties those components to the current application, so major framework parts cannot be reused in a future architecture without first separating out the application-specific logic.
risks.rationale: Reuse in a different architecture requires components free of the original application's logic; the input states the logic is embedded in framework components.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Extent to which application logic is embedded within framework components (AE-1, BD-13)

scenario_reference.text: When a modification to the framework is required during development or maintenance, it is made cost-effectively, fast and in minimal time.

analysis_records.environment: Development/maintenance time (inferred from the change-oriented wording); no condition is stated in RS-7
analysis_records.stimulus: A modification to the framework is required (nature of the change not stated in RS-7)
architectural_decisions: The Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers, with no intermediary described (AP-2, AE-3).
All handlers extend one base Handler (AP-3, AE-5).
Application logic is embedded within framework components (AP-4, AE-1, BD-13).
analysis_records.reasoning: RS-7 is about changes to the framework itself. Inferred: because the Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers (AE-3) and every handler extends the base Handler (AE-5), the Event Manager-to-Handler interface is shared by all application handlers; a change to that interface or to the base Handler propagates to every application-specific handler. Because application logic is embedded within framework components (AE-1, BD-13), modifying a framework component also means touching application logic held inside it. Both widen the set of components affected by a framework change and so raise its cost and time. No cost or time figure is given, so whether the modification is 'cost-effective, fast and in minimal time' cannot be judged (G-2-7, G-4-4). The embedding decision has no stated benefit (G-3-5), so no tradeoff point can be named for it (G-4-11).

risks.description: Framework modifications to the Event Manager or base Handler interface propagate to every application-specific handler, and modifications to framework components touch the application logic embedded in them, raising the cost and time of framework change.
risks.rationale: Direct Event Manager-to-handler interaction (AE-3) with all handlers sharing the base Handler (AE-5), combined with stated high framework-application inter-dependence (AE-1, BD-13), widens change impact.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Interface between the Event Manager and the base Handler (direct interaction, AE-3; shared by all handlers, AE-5)

scenario_reference.text: When framework components interact to process events at runtime, they interact in a coordinated manner.

analysis_records.environment: Runtime; no operating condition is stated in RS-8
analysis_records.stimulus: Framework components interact to handle and process events (business goal BD-2)
architectural_decisions: One Event Queue with FIFO dispatch is the single ordering point for all events (AP-1, AE-4, AE-10, BD-11).
One Event Manager is the sole dispatcher to handlers (AP-2, AE-3, AE-10).
The framework-owned Main drives control flow (AP-5, inferred from AE-2, AE-3, AE-5).
Events are processed sequentially (AP-6, inferred from AE-7).
analysis_records.reasoning: Coordination among components is concentrated in two single instances: every event passes through one FIFO Event Queue and is dispatched by one Event Manager (AE-10, BD-11). Inferred: the dispatch logic therefore exists in one place and every event follows the same Queue -> Manager -> Handler path, so components do not need to coordinate with each other directly. If Main owns the control loop (AP-5, inferred, G-3-1) and processing is sequential (AP-6, inferred, G-3-2), there is also a single execution model. The same FIFO-only ordering means an urgent event cannot overtake earlier ones, which is the opposing performance effect. 'Coordinated' is not defined, so the response cannot be judged against a criterion (G-2-8, G-4-4).

non_risks.description: Dispatch coordination is centralized in one Event Manager reading one FIFO Event Queue, so every event follows the same path and the coordination logic is defined once.
non_risks.rationale: AE-10 limits the architecture to one manager and one queue, BD-11 fixes FIFO dispatch, and AE-3 says the manager interacts directly with handlers; this leaves no second dispatch path that could be inconsistent. The claim that execution is also sequential rests on inferred AP-6 (G-4-5).

sensitivity_points.parameter: Dispatch ordering policy of the Event Queue (cited: FIFO, BD-11)

tradeoff_points.parameter: FIFO-only dispatch policy with no prioritization (BD-11, AP-1); inferred: one ordering rule keeps interaction uniform, but urgent events wait behind all earlier events

scenario_reference.text: When the framework needs to be expanded to allow more sophisticated options, the expansion is possible.

analysis_records.environment: Development/maintenance time (inferred from the change-oriented wording); no condition is stated in RS-9
analysis_records.stimulus: A need to expand the framework to allow more sophisticated options
architectural_decisions: Expansion through new handler subtypes of the base Handler (AP-3, AE-5).
Fixed architecture limits of one Event Manager and one Event Queue (AP-1, AP-2, AE-10).
Application logic embedded within framework components (AP-4, AE-1, BD-13).
analysis_records.reasoning: The 'more sophisticated options' are not named (G-2-9), so only the structural bounds on expansion can be stated. Expansions that take the form of new handlers use the base Handler extension point (see NR-1 in AR-4, same conditions on G-3-6). Inferred: expansions that need more than one queue (for example prioritized queues) or more than one manager change the fixed limits stated in AE-10 and therefore change the framework's core structure rather than adding to it. Expansions that touch application logic embedded in framework components carry the change-scope concern already recorded as R-6. No new risk is recorded because the target options are unknown; recording one would be speculation.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Fixed architecture limits of one Event Manager and one Event Queue (cited: AE-10); expansions needing more queues or managers change these core elements

scenario_reference.text: When the framework's data structures are accessed while the system is running, the data is properly encapsulated and the data structures are secure.

analysis_records.environment: Runtime; no operating condition is stated in RS-11
analysis_records.stimulus: Access to data held in the framework's data structures
architectural_decisions: Application logic is embedded within framework components and is highly inter-dependent with the framework (AP-4, AE-1, BD-13).
Handlers share the base Handler abstraction (AP-3, AE-5).
analysis_records.reasoning: Only the encapsulation half of RS-11 can be analyzed. The input states that application logic is embedded within framework components and that application and framework are highly inter-dependent (AE-1, BD-13). Inferred: no encapsulation boundary between application data and framework data is described; application code living inside framework components can reach the framework's internal data structures. The 'secure data structures' half cannot be analyzed: the inputs describe no data structures, shared state, threats or access-control mechanism (G-3-8, G-3-9, G-4-8). Security is also not among the named architectural drivers (G-2-18).

risks.description: Embedding application logic within framework components (BD-13, AE-1) leaves no described encapsulation boundary between application code and the framework's data structures, contrary to the proper encapsulation RS-11 requires.
risks.rationale: RS-11 requires encapsulation of framework data; the stated embedding and high inter-dependence place application code inside the framework components that hold that data.

scenario_reference.text: When the architecture operates, it exhibits overall consistent behavior.

architectural_decisions: One FIFO Event Queue (AP-1, AE-4, AE-10, BD-11).
Sequential processing on one processor (AP-6, inferred from AE-7).
All handlers conform to one base Handler abstraction (AP-3, AE-5).
Framework-owned Main and STOP handler as uniform control and termination paths (AP-5, AP-8, both inferred).
analysis_records.reasoning: Inferred: with one FIFO queue (AE-10, BD-11) processed sequentially (AP-6, from AE-7), the same input sequence is processed in the same order every time, and because every handler extends the base Handler (AE-5) all handlers are invoked through one abstraction. Together these support consistent behaviour. The sequential model is what removes interleaving; the same choice limits throughput (AE-9 states transactions are slow), so the concurrency model is a tradeoff point. The determinism claim depends on AP-6, which the input calls 'implied' (G-3-2, G-4-5). Uniform control and termination paths would further support consistency, but AP-5 and AP-8 are inferred (G-3-1, G-3-3) and no finding is based on them. 'Consistent behavior' is not defined (G-2-13, G-4-4).

non_risks.description: Sequential processing of a single FIFO Event Queue gives a deterministic processing order for a given input sequence, and all handlers are invoked through one base Handler abstraction, which supports consistent behaviour.
non_risks.rationale: AE-10 and BD-11 give one FIFO queue; AE-7 implies sequential processing; AE-5 gives the common base Handler. Depends on the inferred approach AP-6 (G-4-5).

sensitivity_points.parameter: Concurrency model of event processing (cited: single processor, sequential processing 'implied', AE-7)

tradeoff_points.parameter: Concurrency model of event processing: sequential on one processor (AE-7) versus concurrent handler execution; inferred: sequential processing gives deterministic order and no concurrent access to the queue and handlers, but bounds throughput

scenario_reference.text: When the framework is used to perform its required tasks, it is complete and clear and performs exactly as required.

analysis_records.stimulus: The framework is used to perform its required tasks, such as event processing
architectural_decisions: A single Event Queue dispatching FIFO (AP-1) for the FIFO dispatch constraint (BD-11).
An Event Manager delivering events to handlers (AP-2, AE-3) for the goal of handling and processing events (BD-2).
CLI input with idle wait until input arrives (AP-7, AE-6) for the idle-state constraints (BD-5, BD-12).
A STOP handler for termination (AP-8, inferred) for the termination constraint (BD-4).
analysis_records.reasoning: The full functional requirements behind 'exactly as required' are not supplied (G-2-14), so only the stated constraints can be checked. Inferred: the FIFO dispatch constraint (BD-11) is matched by the single Event Queue (AP-1), the idle-wait-until-input constraints (BD-5, BD-12) by the CLI idle-wait approach (AP-7), and the event-handling goal (BD-2) by the Event Manager delivering events to handlers (AE-3). These are matches between stated constraints and described components, not verified behaviour; the class diagrams and interaction descriptions that would confirm them were not supplied (AE-12, G-1-3). The STOP-handler constraint (BD-4) cannot be checked because AP-8 is inferred and no AE item describes the STOP handler (G-3-3, G-4-9). Completeness and clarity cannot be judged without the requirements (G-4-4).

non_risks.description: The single FIFO Event Queue (AP-1) and the CLI idle-wait input approach (AP-7) correspond to the stated FIFO dispatch constraint (BD-11) and idle-state constraints (BD-5, BD-12).
non_risks.rationale: Each stated constraint has a described component that realizes it; marked inferred because the inputs state these as constraints and the documentation that would confirm the implementation was not supplied (AE-12, G-1-3).

scenario_reference.text: When multiple applications are hooked up to the framework at the same time, the framework accommodates them.

analysis_records.environment: Not stated in RS-15 whether this is at development, deployment or runtime
analysis_records.stimulus: Multiple applications are hooked up to the framework at the same time
architectural_decisions: One Event Manager and one Event Queue (AP-1, AP-2, AE-10).
The Main module is part of the framework (AP-5, AE-2).
Application logic is embedded within framework components (AP-4, AE-1, BD-13).
analysis_records.reasoning: AE-10 limits the framework to one Event Manager and one Event Queue, Main belongs to the framework (AE-2), and application logic is embedded within framework components (AE-1, BD-13). Inferred: within one framework instance, several applications hooked up at once would share one queue, one manager and one Main, and the inputs describe no mechanism to separate their events or route them to the right application's handlers (G-3-6); because each application's logic is embedded in the framework components, running several applications appears to require either mixing their logic in the same components or running separate framework instances. If RS-15 means build-time support of several applications rather than simultaneous runtime hook-up, the concern is weaker; the phase is not stated (G-2-15). The ownership of the control loop by Main is part of inferred AP-5 (G-3-1, G-4-6).

risks.description: With one Event Manager, one Event Queue and one framework-owned Main (AE-10, AE-2), and application logic embedded in framework components (BD-13), no mechanism is described for separating the events and handlers of several applications hooked up at the same time.
risks.rationale: RS-15 requires accommodating multiple simultaneous applications, which needs some separation or routing mechanism; the fixed single instances and the embedding leave none described (G-3-6).

sensitivity_points.parameter: Number of Event Managers and Event Queues per framework instance (cited: 1 each, AE-10)

scenario_reference.text: When a change of the interface from command-driven to window-based is requested during development or maintenance, the interface is changed.

analysis_records.environment: Development/maintenance time (inferred); the system currently accepts input via CLI (AE-6)
analysis_records.stimulus: A request to change the interface from command-driven to window-based
architectural_decisions: Input is taken via the CLI and the system idles until input is received (AP-7, AE-6, BD-5, BD-12).
The Main module, which presumably owns the control loop, is part of the framework (AP-5, AE-2; control-loop ownership inferred).
Events reach handlers through the Event Queue and Event Manager (AP-1, AE-3, AE-4).
analysis_records.reasoning: Inferred: handlers receive events from the Event Manager (AE-3) reading the Event Queue (AE-4), not from the CLI directly, so handler code need not change if a window-based front end produces the same events; this rests on the event-dispatch reading of AP-9 and on the undisclosed binding mechanism (G-3-4, G-3-6). However, the idle-wait-until-input behaviour is stated as a framework constraint (BD-5, BD-12), Main belongs to the framework (AE-2), and no input component or abstraction separating the input source from the Event Queue is named. Inferred: the CLI-specific waiting and reading appear to sit in framework-owned control flow, so moving to a window-based interface may require changing Main and the idle-wait logic rather than only adding an input component. This depends on inferred AP-5 (G-3-1, G-4-6). No effort or scope limit is stated (G-2-16, G-4-4).

risks.description: No input abstraction is described between the CLI and the Event Queue, and the idle-wait-until-input behaviour (BD-5, BD-12) belongs to framework-owned control flow (Main, AE-2), so replacing the CLI with a window-based interface may require changing the framework's Main and idle-wait logic.
risks.rationale: AE-6 fixes CLI input, BD-5/BD-12 require idle wait in the framework, AE-2 places Main in the framework; no AE item names a replaceable input component. Depends on inferred AP-5 (G-4-6).

non_risks.description: Application handlers receive events through the Event Queue and Event Manager rather than reading the CLI directly, so handler code need not change if a window-based front end produces the same events.
non_risks.rationale: AE-3 and AE-4 place the Event Manager and Queue between input and handlers. Conditional on the event-dispatch reading of AP-9 and the undisclosed handler binding (G-3-4, G-3-6, G-4-7).

sensitivity_points.parameter: Coupling between the input source (CLI, AE-6) and the framework-owned Main/idle-wait control loop (AE-2, BD-12)

gaps.description: RS-12 (implementation using other programming languages) could not be analyzed: the current language, target languages and the language features the design relies on (e.g. whether handler extension of the base Handler, AE-5, is class inheritance) are not stated.
gaps.missing_evidence: Current implementation language, target languages (G-2-12) and the mechanism by which handlers extend the base Handler
gaps.resolution_question: In which language is the framework implemented, which languages must it be re-implementable in, and does handler extension depend on class inheritance?

gaps.description: No analyzed scenario has a response measure, so no record can judge whether its response is achieved; findings state direction of effect only. Affected: AR-1/RS-2 (G-2-2), AR-2/RS-3 (G-2-3), AR-3/RS-4 (G-2-4), AR-4/RS-5 (G-2-5), AR-5/RS-6 (G-2-6), AR-6/RS-7 (G-2-7), AR-7/RS-8 (G-2-8), AR-8/RS-9 (G-2-9), AR-9/RS-11 (G-2-11), AR-10/RS-13 (G-2-13), AR-11/RS-14 (G-2-14), AR-12/RS-15 (G-2-15), AR-13/RS-16 (G-2-16).
gaps.missing_evidence: Measurable response measures for each scenario (e.g. latency or component-count target for RS-2, recovery time for RS-3, change effort for RS-5/RS-7/RS-16)
gaps.resolution_question: What measurable response does each of these scenarios require, so the findings can be judged as met or not met?

gaps.description: Findings R-2, NR-2 (in part), NR-3 and T-4 depend on AP-6 (sequential single-processor processing), which 03_approaches.json marks inferred because the input calls it 'implied' (AE-7, G-3-2).
gaps.missing_evidence: Statement of the threading/concurrency model of event processing
gaps.resolution_question: Are events strictly processed one at a time on one thread, or can handlers run concurrently? If concurrent, R-2, NR-3 and T-4 must be revised.

gaps.description: Findings R-10 (in part), R-11 and S-14 depend on AP-5 (framework-owned Main driving the control loop), which is inferred from AE-2, AE-3 and AE-5 (G-3-1).
gaps.missing_evidence: Main module responsibilities, location of the idle-wait/CLI read loop, and whether an input component separates the input source from the Event Queue
gaps.resolution_question: Where is the CLI read and idle-wait logic located, in Main or in a separate input component, and does Main own the event loop?

gaps.description: NR-1, NR-5 and S-6 depend on how handlers are bound to events (G-3-6) and on the event-dispatch reading of AP-9 (inferred, G-3-4). If dispatch is hard-coded in the Event Manager, adding a handler also changes the manager and NR-1 weakens.
gaps.missing_evidence: Handler registration/binding mechanism and the event-type catalogue
gaps.resolution_question: How does the Event Manager select the handler for an event, and does adding a new application-specific handler require editing the Event Manager?

gaps.description: Only the encapsulation part of RS-11 was analyzed (R-9); the 'secure data structures' part could not be analyzed because no data structures, shared state, threats or data-protection mechanisms are described (G-3-8, G-3-9).
gaps.missing_evidence: Inventory of framework data structures, which components share them, and any protection mechanism
gaps.resolution_question: Which data structures does the framework hold or share between handlers, and how are they protected from application code?

gaps.description: AR-11 (RS-14) could check only the stated constraints BD-5, BD-11 and BD-12; the STOP-handler termination constraint (BD-4) could not be checked because AP-8 is inferred and no AE item describes the STOP handler (G-3-3), and the full functional requirements are absent (G-2-14).
gaps.missing_evidence: STOP handler description (trigger, dispatch path) and the framework's functional requirements
gaps.resolution_question: How is the STOP handler triggered and dispatched, and which functional requirements define 'performs exactly as required'?

gaps.description: T-1 attributes the high number of components per transaction (AE-9) to the handler decomposition that supports variability and modifiability (AP-3); the input names the proxy but not which components a transaction passes through or how many.
gaps.missing_evidence: The component path of a typical transaction and its component count
gaps.resolution_question: Which components does a typical event pass through from CLI input to handler completion, and could that number be reduced without losing the handler extension point?

gaps.description: AP-4 (application logic embedded in framework components) is implicated in R-4, R-6, R-7, R-8, R-9 and R-10, but no tradeoff point could be recorded for it because the inputs state no quality benefit of the embedding (G-3-5).
gaps.missing_evidence: Design rationale for embedding application logic in framework components
gaps.resolution_question: What quality goal, if any (e.g. simplicity or speed of development), did embedding application logic in framework components serve?

gaps.description: The severity of R-3 depends on whether events in the single Event Queue survive a failure; persistence of queue contents and framework state is not described (G-3-9).
gaps.missing_evidence: Whether the Event Queue and framework state are persisted, and what state the system restarts in
gaps.resolution_question: Is the Event Queue held only in memory, and what happens to queued events and handler state when the system fails?
